Seminar Title:

Lime Pumice Calcined Clay Binder: Development of Durable and Low-Carbon Cementitious Material

Abstract:

Ancient Roman concrete is an extremely durable cementitious material that has lasted for millennia in harsh environments, particularly marine conditions. The extraordinary durability and longevity of ancient Roman concrete have inspired scientific interest in its use as an alternative to ordinary Portland cement (OPC) in modern construction. Extensive literature demonstrates a series of pozzolanic and post-pozzolanic reactions in Roman seawater concrete, forming C-S-H and C-(A)-S-H, with a key set of binding minerals, such as Al-tobermorite, stratlingite, hydrogarnet, and zeolites, thereby increasing its serviceability. It was observed that Al-tobermorite primarily contributes to early-age strength, and these hydrated products are further enhanced by prolonged exposure to seawater, a behaviour significantly different from that of OPC binding phases.

This research presents a novel pathway to recreate the cementitious materials of Roman concrete by combining hydrated lime with natural pozzolanas, such as pumice (PU) and calcined clay (CC), and using natural seawater closely resembling that used by the Romans. First, pozzolanic reactivity assessment tests based on various testing standards were conducted to determine the reactivity of CC and PU individually and in various blends. Based on the reactivity assessment, a systematic methodology was used to prepare a series of batches with variable lime-to-pozzolana ratios (1:2 to 1:4) and CC-to-PU ratios of 100:0, 50:50, and 75:25. The optimum seawater-to-binder (Hydrated lime to natural pozzolana) ratio was then selected based on a trial-and-error method. Specimens of 50mm size were cast and cured in natural seawater. At specific time points, the paste samples were removed from the seawater, and their compressive strength was measured. The evolution of the reaction products and the microstructural properties of the paste samples were analysed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and Scanning Electron Microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS). Overall, this composite binder offers a potential pathway for producing durable, low-carbon cementitious materials primarily using natural pozzolans, underscoring the importance of utilising naturally abundant resources, such as clay, pumice, and seawater.&nbsp
